Emotions

What is sadness for?

Nobody wants to feel sad, but sadness serves useful purposes. Telling it apart from depression matters.

We live in a culture that places great value on feeling good, and sadness is sometimes treated as a fault to be fixed as soon as possible. But it is a basic emotion we share with other mammals, and emotions that have survived evolution usually serve some purpose.

What sadness does

Sadness tends to arise after a loss or when something does not go as we hoped. It slows us down, makes us withdraw and think about what happened. That brake can be useful: it helps us review events and adjust our plans. The expression of sadness also stirs a wish to help in others.

The psychologist Joseph Forgas has found in several experiments that a mildly sad mood can improve some tasks: people recall details more accurately, are less gullible about rumours and judge with fewer stereotypes. This does not mean being sad is better, but that each mood favours a different style of thinking.

Sadness is not depression

Sadness has a reason, comes and goes, and usually still allows us to enjoy some things. Depression is more persistent: it lasts most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks, and comes with loss of interest, changes in sleep or appetite, tiredness, feelings of guilt or worthlessness and difficulty concentrating.

Crying

As far as we know, humans are the only animals that cry from emotion. Ad Vingerhoets, who has studied crying for decades, argues that its main function is social: tears signal that we need help and draw care from others. Whether crying brings relief depends a lot on the situation: it tends to feel better when someone is with us and comforts us, and less so when we feel judged.

Sadness in other cultures

Not all cultures value sadness in the same way. In some traditions, such as Portuguese saudade or Japanese mono no aware, a certain melancholy is seen as beautiful and deep. In societies that push people to be positive all the time, by contrast, feeling sad can also bring guilt for not being fine. Brock Bastian's studies suggest that this pressure not to feel negative emotions is associated with more depressive symptoms.

What usually helps

  • Allow yourself to be sad for a while, without forcing a cheerfulness you do not feel.
  • Share it with someone you trust.
  • Keep some routine: sleeping, eating and moving help keep your mood from sinking.
If sadness lasts for weeks, stops you functioning or thoughts of death appear, see your doctor. If you are thinking of ending your life, please contact a crisis line in your country (in Spain, 024).

References

  1. Forgas, J. P. (2013). Don't worry, be sad! On the cognitive, motivational, and interpersonal benefits of negative mood. Current Directions in Psychological Science, 22(3), 225–232.
  2. American Psychiatric Association (2022). DSM-5-TR. Trastorno de depresión mayor.
  3. Vingerhoets, A. (2013). Why Only Humans Weep. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
